events.event_narrative: Snow fell heavily at times during the afternoon and evening hours of the 16th. By the morning of the 17th, the department of highways estimated 6 to 7 inches of accumulation along the Highway 504 corridor in northwest Elliot County. Lesser amounts of around 4 inches were estimated in the eastern part of the county along Highway 32 near the Elliot/Lawrence county line. A CoCoRaHS observer reported 4.1 inches of snow 9 miles south southeast of Olive Hill at 9:00 AM on the 17th.

Snow showers with embedded squalls developed on the afternoon of the 28th, and continued into the morning hours of the 29th. Snowfall amounts across the county were locally enhanced due to upslope flow, leading to widely varying tallies. Atop Big Black Mountain along KY-160, the highway department reported 4.0 inches at 1130 PM on 28th. By 8 AM on the 29th, this had increased to an estimated 9.0 inches. Elsewhere across the county, the highway department estimated a 3 to 4 inch snow total around Harlan and about 6 inches near Cumberland. The Lynch post office estimated a 6.5 inch storm total snowfall.

As of 2:10 PM EST, an NWS Employee measured 4.6 inches 1 mile WSW of Stanton, with snow still falling. An hour later, totals were ranging between 4.3 inches (community of Nada) and 6.0 inches (1 mile S of Stanton). By the end of the event, 7.3 inches of storm total snowfall was reported 1 mile WSW of Stanton.

Storm total snow for Bath County, KY measured an average of 4.0 inches for the county. There were reports from the emergency manager that 25 to 30 cars went off the road on Interstate 64 through the county.

Both a public reporter in the community of Stony Fork and a trained spotter in Beverly reported 4.0 inches of storm total snowfall. Stony Fork reported 4 inches as of 5:30 PM EST, while Beverly reached that amount approximately an hour earlier.

Maximum storm total snowfall of 6.5 inches reported at 1 mile S of Paxton, KY from an NWS employee. Storm total snowfall averaged between 5.5 inches and 6.5 inches across the county. The National Weather Service office also reported 5.7 inches of storm total snowfall.
The city of Manchester reached 5.0 inches of snowfall at 5:28 PM EST.
The Elliott County 911 Dispatch Center in Sandy Hook reported 6.0 inches of snowfall as of 5:33 PM EST.

The maximum snowfall for the event was 8.5 inches, measured 1 mile SSE of Spout Springs by a member of the public. Other reports across the county also topped 7.0 inches, including a measurement of 7.0 inches from an Emergency Manager in Irvine.
A trained spotter reported 4.0 inches of storm total snowfall through 6:37 PM EST, located 3 miles west of Wallingford.

At 5:00pm EST, a trained spotter located 1 mile West of Dotson had received 4.0 inches. By 7:45pm EST, the same location had accumulated another 3.5 inches, bringing their storm total snowfall to 7.4 inches. Just down the road, a cooperative observer located 2 miles ENE of Dotson received 7.1 inches of snow. The community of Harold also reported a storm total snowfall of 6.0 inches.

The Department of Highways reported 6.0 inches of storm total snowfall 1 mile east of Black Mountain. The remainder of the county averaged between 5.0 and 6.0 inches based on reports from the Department of Highways.
The maximum snowfall report for the event was in Sandgap, where 6.0 inches was reported by the Department of Highways. Meanwhile, McKee had received 5.0 inches at the same report time.
The maximum snowfall report was 7.8 inches, coming from both Paintsville and 1 mile SW of Hager Hill.
A storm total report of 4.0 inches was received from the State Police Patrol Post in Hindman, KY at 5:57 PM EST.
A public observer in the community of Bimble reported 6.5 inches of snow as of 6:05 PM EST.
East Bernstadt saw a storm total snowfall of 6.6 inches by Thursday evening.  Totals ranged between 5.8 and 6.6 inches throughout the county.
A maximum snowfall report of 6.0 inches was measured in Beattyville, KY by the 911 Call Center.
A spotter located 1 mile ESE of Kaliopi measured 5.5 inches of storm total snowfall at 6:22 PM EST.

A maximum snowfall amount of 6.5 inches was reported 1 mile N of Oven Fork, along the crest of Pine Mountain on US-119 by the Dept. of Highway. Meanwhile, a trained spotter located 1 mile NNW of Farraday received 4.5 inches as of 7:22 PM EST.
Hendricks measured 5.5 inches of storm total snowfall through 5:39 PM EST on January 6. Another similar report of 5.0 inches was received out of the Gunlock Community at 5:00 PM EST.
Dispatch and Emergency Management reported a storm total snowfall of 7.0 inches in the community of Inez. Meanwhile, an hour before, the community of Warfield reported 6.0 inches of snow.
The maximum storm total snowfall amount reported was 5.5 inches in Whitley City, KY from a member of the public.
A Storm total snowfall of 6.5 inches was reported in Frenchburg, KY by the fire department.
Just before 3:00 PM EST, the community of Oggs Station had a report of 5.5 inches of snow. By the end of the event, they had accumulated a storm total snowfall of 7.6 inches.
A storm total snowfall amount of 6.0 inches was reported in West Liberty, KY from a 911 Call Center. Much of Morgan County averaged around 6 inches as well.
A storm total snowfall of 4.3 inches was reported in Chestnut Gap, KY from an emergency manager. Snow was fairly uniform throughout the county.
A maximum snowfall amount of 4.0 inches was reported in Frew/Big Creek, KY from an amateur radio report. Another 4.0 inch report was received from the Perry County 911 at 5:30 PM EST.

A maximum storm total snowfall amount of 6.0 inches was reported in Pikeville, KY from the 911 Call Center. Elsewhere across the county, amounts ranged from 3 inches (3 miles west of Mouthcard) to 6 inches.
A maximum snowfall amount of 7.0 inches was reported in Quinton, KY from a public report.  Storm total snowfall averaged 6.0 to 7.0 inches through the county.
The Rockcastle County Dispatch Center in Mount Vernon had received 4.5 inches of snowfall 6:01 PM EST.
Maximum snowfall amount of 6.8 inches was reported in Hilda, KY. One mile south of Morehead had a similar amount of 6.0 inches.
Monticello reported 4.5 inches of storm total snowfall as of 5:11 PM EST.
A storm total snowfall of 5.0 inches was reported in 1 mile northeast of Corbin. Elsewhere, Clio reported 4.5 inches of storm total snowfall.
Maximum storm total snowfall amount of 6.0 inches was reported in Toliver, KY from an NWS employee. Much of the county averaged around the same amount.
Maximum amount of snow is estimated to be 4.0 inches on Black and Pine Mountains from the Highway Department. Total snowfall is averaged 2.0 inches for the remainder of Harlan County.
Maximum amount of snow is estimated to be 4.0 inches on Pine Mountains from the Highway Department. Total snowfall is averaged 2.0 inches for the remainder of Letcher County.

A NWS Employee located 3 miles north of Stanton (near the Montgomery County line) estimated 0.25 inches of ice accumulations on the trees at 7:00 AM EST. A couple hours later, at 9:15 AM EST, the Department of Highways reported over 0.25 inches of ice on elevated surfaces 1 mile SW of Stanton.
The Bath County Emergency Manager reported 0.25 inches of ice accumulation near the community of Owingsville by 7am EST, Friday.
At 8:25am EST, the Emergency Manager reported greater than 0.25 inches of ice measured at the Fleming County EOC in Flemingsburg.
The Emergency Manager in Rowan County reported 0.25 inches of ice on elevated surfaces near the community of Clearfield as of 9:30 am EST.

The Williamsburg Airport AWOS recorded a peak wind gust of 51 knots (59 mph) at 1:15 AM EST on the 31st. Numerous gusts in excess of 40 mph were recorded between 11:55 PM EST, March 30th and 2:35 AM EST, March 31st. A local utility company reported that the winds had blown multiple trees onto power lines along Hightop Rd (approximately 2 miles SE of Rye) and snapped two 3-phase power poles.

Sporadic large tree damage was reported across the county. The McCreary County dispatch reported that strong wind gusts had blown down a large tree onto a road around 6:49 PM on the 30th, approximately 3 miles NNW of Hollyhill. At 10:30 PM another large tree was reportedly blocking Lum-Strunk Rd. A third report of a large tree blocking Williamsburg was estimated to have occurred around 3:50 AM on the 31st.

Estill County dispatch reported sporadic trees blown down onto roadways. The first downed tree was reported at 7:47 PM EST on the 31st along Cobb Fork about 1 miles ESE of Fox. Additional trees was reportedly blown down onto Sandhill Rd. near Weedon at 11:40 PM, and on Hood Avenue in Irvine around 12:29 AM.

Sporadic tree damage was observed around the county. A tree was reportedly blown down onto the bed of a pickup truck around 10:55 PM EST in Burnside. County dispatch reported a large tree blown down across Estesburg Rd at 11:15 PM, approximately 3 NNE of Pulaski. Another large tree was blown down across Melvin Church Rd. Power lines were knocked down by trees 3 WSW of Alpine.

Powell County dispatch reported sporadic tree damage across the county. A tree was reportedly blown down onto power lines, taking them down as well, approximately 1 ENE of Stanton at 11:45 PM EST, March 30th. Additional reports of trees blown down onto Thorpe Ridge, Cane Creek, and Black Creek roads were received early on the 31st.

Strong winds led to sporadic tree damage. County dispatch reported a tree down onto a power line at approximately 12:35 AM EST on the 31st. A large tree was also blown down onto the intersection of Bedford and Tabor roads. An NWS Employee near Hope reported that nearly all of the trusses on a large barn, which was under construction, were blown over.

County dispatch reported several trees blown down along Cooper Creek and Sweetwater roads. A local utility company also reported that a power pole along Hidden Valley Road had been broken by a falling tree. A personal weather station at nearby Wabo measured a 54 mph peak wind gust at 1:24 AM.
A local utility company reported that multiple trees were blown down onto power lines and broke a 3-phase power pole along KY-3483.
The local utility company reported multiple broken power poles and numerous small power outages due to trees falling on power lines. Broken poles were located along Hounchell Rd. and Liberty Rd.

The local electric company reported that falling trees snapped 3 power poles in a row along KY-1803 at New Bethel. A church adjacent to the down power lines had its roof blown off. County dispatch reported numerous small power outages and trees on lines throughout the county. The county judge executive indicated that multiple carports and other similar structures were displaced.
Pictures on social media showed roofing blown off of a small home near Hazel Green. Another picture showed roofing removed from a structure in the Lacy Creek area.

The local utility company reported that a large tree had been blown down onto and damaged a double circuit adjacent to the substation, located 1/2 miles west of city of Booneville, causing a major power outage across much of the county. Two other power poles, one up the left hand fork of Cow Creek and the other near Vincent, were snapped due to large trees falling onto the power lines. Otherwise, the emergency manager reported a number of small power outages around the county due to fallen trees. The extensive damage required the electric company to call in additional assistance from outside the area.

The county emergency manager reported that a barn along Improvement Fork Rd. had collapsed due to strong winds, and also that trees had been blown down along Ivy Point Rd. and US-460 at Bear Branch Rd. Local dispatch reported that multiple trees were blown down on US-460, 0.8 miles west of Salyersville, and also directly across KY-7 within the city limits.

The ASOS at the NWS in Jackson reported a wind gust of 51 mph at 2:03 AM EST, March 31st. Pictures on social media showed a tree blown down, and damage to the roof of a house and barn, 2 miles ESE of Guerrant.

The local utility company reported that a tree had fallen onto power lines and snapped a power pole along Old Way Rd approximately 2 miles NNE of Brock. The nearby ASOS at the London Corbin Airport clocked a peak gust of 48 knots (55 mph) at 11:53 PM EST, March 30th.
The public reported that strong winds had blown down a large tree across Lost Creek Road a couple miles east southeast of Dice.
County dispatch reported that a tree was blown down and blocked one lane of KY-1274. Another tree was blown down onto power lines at the intersection of Sulphur Springs and Cope Ridge roads.

The local utility company reported that multiple trees were blown down onto power lines along KY-221 near the junction of KY-1780. The trees broke the cross arms on 3 power poles which allowed the lines to fall on the ground.
Numerous trees were blown down by thunderstorm wind gusts throughout the county, particularly in and around Whitley City.

The Highway Department reported multiple trees down across the county between 10:45pm and 11pm EST. Roads impacted by downed trees included KY-421 near the Boho community, KY-638 near the Sidell community, KY-11 near the community of Tanksley, and KY-3477 near US-421 just SSE of the Fall Rock community.

The Highway Department reported multiple trees down across the county between 11:43pm and 12:05am EST. Roads impacted by downed trees included KY-221 between the intersection with Evelyn Lane and Mill Branch Church Loop, KY-1780 between the intersections with Salt Trace Branch Road and Middle Fork Road, KY-990 near the intersection with Engle Road, and KY-987 just east of the intersection with Laurel Branch.
The Highway Department reported a tree down due to high winds along KY-76, near the intersection with KY-899.

The Highway Department reported two trees down across the county between 11:22pm and 11:30pm EST. Roads impacted by downed trees included Francis Branch Road near the community of Ned, and KY-28 between mile markers 13 and 14.
The Highway Department reported a tree down due to high winds on Red Lick Road, near the intersection with Station Camp Road.
A tree was reported down on Mountain Crest Circle near the intersection with Grindstone Road in North Irvine.
A car port was reported having been blown over onto Richmond Road near the intersection with Pea Ridge Road.
The highway department reported a tree down across KY-1028 between mile marker 3 and 4.
The highway department reported a tree down across KY-1057 around mile marker 2.
The highway department reported a tree down across KY-213 around mile marker 6 near Stanton, KY.
Dispatch reported that a tree was down on Hardwicks Creek Road near the community of Vaughns Mill.
A public report from Marshes Siding, Kentucky reported multiple trees down due to the gust front.
A tree was reported down on Natural Bridge Road near Natural Bridge State Park.
A tree was reported down on Cane Creek Road, near the community of Rosslyn.
The Department of Highways reported 0.25 inches of freezing rain/ice in Sandy Hook at 8:30am EST.
A tree was reported down, blocking KY-52 at Reges Road. Another tree was blown down onto powerlines on Reges Road.
A NWS Employee located 3 miles north of Stanton (near the Powell County line) estimated 0.25 inches of ice accumulation on the trees at 7:00 AM EST.

Powell County dispatch reported that a house off of Darrell Randall Rd in Stanton, Kentucky had its roof blown off, as well as a vehicle damaged from the roof. ||WKYT in Lexington also reported on this story. The information can be found at: https://www.wymt.com/2022/04/18/it-sounded-like-house-was-going-blow-apart-eastern-kentucky-family-cleaning-up-after-strong-storms-dealt-severe-damage/ .
Some roofing, shingles, and siding damage was reported to a home from gusty winds near West Liberty.
Red Lick Road (KY-3328) was reported blocked due to flooding between mile markers 0 and 1.3.
KY-52 was reported being blocked due to floodwaters between mile markers 0 and 2 in Lee County.
KY-711 near the community of Wrigley was reported as being blocked due to flood waters, between mile markers 3 and 4.
North KY-11 in Heidrick was reported blocked due to flood waters between mile markers 11 and 12.
KY-1527 was reported blocked due to flood waters between mile markers 0 and 1 near the community of Baileys Switch.
KY-2013 was reported blocked due to flood waters in the community of Jenson.
KY-1527 was reported blocked due to flooding in the area between mile markers 2 and 2.4 in the community of Baileys Switch.
KY-225 was blocked due to flooding in the area at mile marker 4, near the community of Kayjay.
Quarter size hail occurred in Hardy.
A tree was blown down on KY State Route 3337, 1.8 miles from KY-30.
Thunderstorm wind gusts partially damaged the roofs of both a barn and a shed off of Ingram Creek Road near Linefork.
A tree was blown down onto a home, briefly trapping the occupants inside. They were freed shortly after by emergency crews. No injuries were reported.
A tree was blown down and onto a road near Jarvis, temporarily blocking the road.
Siding was partially removed from a residence by a thunderstorm wind gust.
Large tree limbs were blown down in near the Happy Church in the Quicksand community.

A trained spotter located in the Beverly area of Bell County gave more than one report while the event was ongoing. These reports indicated higher snowfall rates were experienced in that area, with the snowfall total going from 1.8 inches to 3.3 inches between 2:00 AM EST and 2:59 AM EST. In addition, the spotter gave a storm total snowfall amount of 8.0 inches at the end of the most impactful snowfall later in the morning, at 8:15 AM EST.
Numerous trees were blown down countywide by thunderstorm wind gusts.

An EF-1 tornado touched down 1 mile west of the Cumberland Falls State Park on Highway 90 and continued into Whitley County and across the park. Wind speeds with this tornado were estimated at 105 mph. Significant damage was done to the park supervisor's residence. Extensive numbers of large trees were blown across roads which made access to parts of the park impossible until they were cleared away. Numerous trees were snapped or uprooted with some of the trees falling on cars and powerlines.

Park officials reported that numerous trees had been blown down by straight line winds. Some trees fell on occupired cabins, cars, and the Cumberland Falls State Park gift shop. Numerous minor injuries were reported, none of which required medical attention.
One large tree was snapped off near its base by thunderstorm wind gusts.
A 5 inch diameter tree limb was blown down by thunderstorm wind gusts.
Utility poles and power lines were blown down along Cumberland Falls Highway or 18th Street.
Numerous trees were blown down on Highway 377.
Numerous tree branches were torn off along Spout Springs Road. Branches were 2 to 5 inches in diameter. One tree was also blown down on Highway 2001.
Numerous trees were blown down county wide, blocking roads. Worst hit area was between Mount Sterling and Jefferson. Camargo was also hit hard.
Nickel size hail was observed.
The roof was blown off an old post office building on Highway 421. Several trees were also blown down.
Numerous tree branches between 2 and 5 inches in diameter were blown down on Highway 52. A couple of trees were also split down the middle and had to be removed from the roadway.
A large tree was blown down onto a tractor crushing it. Numerous large limbs and a couple of other large trees were also blown down.
Golf ball size hail fell for about 3 minutes.
Nickel size hail fell for one to two minutes. A wind gust estimated at 50 mph brought down several two to three inch diameter tree limbs and an eight inch diameter tree.
Golf ball size hail fell for nearly 5 minutes at Hell For Certain.
Two trees were blown down. Numerous tree branches were also blown down.
Numerous trees were blown down across a fifty foot wide by one quarter mile long path.
A 59 mph wind gust was measured by the Triangle Mountain RAWS observation platform.
Penny size hail fell for 5 minutes.
Numerous trees were blown down from West Liberty to Ezel.
Nickel size hail fell at the NWS office at the airport. The event lasted for 4 minutes.
Several trees and large limbs were blown down.
An EF-1 tornado with wind speeds of around 95 mph briefly touched down one mile southeast of Wooton. Large trees were either snapped off or blown over. One tree fell onto a power line.

One CoCoRaHS report was received near the beginning of the event. This report stated that 2 inches of snow fell within a 75 minute period ending at 12:28am EST, revealing parts of the county were experiencing higher snowfall rates around this time. Storm total reports 15 miles WSW of Somerset and in the community of Science Hill ranged from 4.5 to 5 inches by the morning hours.

Heavier snowfall rates were confirmed near the beginning of the event, with one trained spotter giving a report of 2.2 inches near 2 am EST on the 12th. 1.9 inches of that total was reported to have fallen since midnight EST on the 12th. Another trained spotter in central Estill County, measured 3.1 inches at 2:20 am EST on the 12th. A COOP observer in northern Estill County reported a storm total of 6.0 inches at 8am EST.

One report was given overnight from a trained spotter that measured 2.8 inches near 3 am EST on the 12th. Storm totals were reported by COOP observers, with 3.3 inches near Stanton at 8am EST, and 5.0 inches further into the western third of the county near Clay City as of 7:00am EST.

Received a report of 3.0 inches (2 SSW of Lakesville) at 3:21am EST and a report of 6.0 inches (Salyersville) at 5:33am EST from the public out of central Magoffin County. A COOP observer at the Salyersville Water Works reported a storm total snowfall of 4.5 inches at 8am EST.

One of the earliest reports came from the public in northern Perry County, where 3.0 inches had fallen as of 3:35am EST. By 5:33am EST, a report came from broadcast media that 6.0 inches had fallen at their studios in Hazard. The highest snowfall amounts reported, between 8.0 and 8.2 inches near Hazard, came from a COOP observer and a trained spotter at 7 and 8am EST, respectively.

After the event had concluded, the emergency manager reported an estimated 5.0 inches in Mount Sterling. He also estimated that areas north of Interstate 64 received 4.0-6.0 inches while locations near the border with Powell County received closer to 6 inches or more. Reports from a CoCoRaHS observer as well as a NWS employee backed up these totals. A COOP observer just north of Mount Sterling did report a smaller total of 3.0 inches as of 7 AM EST.

As of 7am EST, snowfall amounts ranged from 3.0 inches 1 mile ENE of Inez, to 7.1 inches 5 WSW of Pilgrim. Later in the morning, at 11:30am EST, another report was sent in from Inez proper, with a measurement of 7.5 inches.
A public report from overnight stated 3.5 inches of snow had been measured at 2:10am EST in Mount Vernon, central Rockcastle County.
Early morning snowfall reports ranged from 3.8 inches as of 6:15am EST in Regina, to 5.5 inches at 5:27am EST in Canada. By 9am EST, 6.0 inches was reported WSW of Mouthcard.

A public report out of Bimble stated 4.3 inches of snow had fallen by 3:56 am EST. A little further to the west, in Barbourville, a public report of 5.8 inches came in around two hours later at 5:57 am EST.

Two snowfall reports were received in the middle of the event. One report was for 4.5 inches (4:44am EST) in the northern portion of the county, and the other gave 5.5 inches (5:43am EST) in the southern sections of the county. More reports came later in the morning with storm totals from across the county ranging from 5.8 to 7.0 inches.
Received one report giving a storm total of 4.5 inches near Monticello as of 7am EST.
A storm total snowfall of 5.0 inches was reported in Blue Heron at 9am EST.
A storm total snowfall of 5.0 inches was reported both in London and in Keavy (public observation) at the end of the event.
A report was received from 8 miles west of McKee at 8am EST with a storm total snowfall of 5.1 inches.

One report from 6:20 EST gave 7.0 inches of snow in Williamsburg. Two more reports came in over the next couple of hours, one from the public and one from a CoCoRaHS observer, with storm total snowfall amounts of 5.3 inches (2 miles south of Walden) and 6.1 inches (7 miles SW of Corbin), respectively.

At 8:40am EST, an NWS employee reported 5.5 inches of snow in the community of Dumont. Light snow continued to fall after this point. By the end of the event, multiple reports of between 6.3 and 6.7 inches of storm total snowfall were reported (NWS Office, Quicksand, and northern Breathitt County - 9 SE of Campton).
A NWS employee reported a storm total of 5.6 inches in the northeastern part of Wolfe County at 9:37am EST.

A total of 5.7 inches was reported by a CoCoRaHS observer in northwest Fleming County at 7am EST on March 12, while a total of 7.9 inches was reported by a trained spotter near Flemingsburg later in the day at 12:55pm EST.
A total of 6.0 inches was reported by the public at 6:15 AM EST in southern Menifee County.
A COOP observer reported a total of 6.0 inches near Paintsville at 7am EST.

At 7:00 AM EST, a COOP Observer near Cave Run Lake reported a total of 6.0 inches. Two more reports were received near the same time, listing totals of 8.0 and 8.1 inches. The former was a public report from near Haldeman and the latter was a CoCoRaHS observer located 6 miles northeast of Morehead.

Thunderstorm winds led to the destruction of 2 barns on a private property. The barns were old, and were not anchored down to the ground. One barn was moved off its foundation by about 15 feet and collapsed. The other lost roofing material and had multiple north-facing wall panels blown off.

Multiple barns and farm structures (corn crib bin and chicken coop) were damaged or destroyed due to thunderstorm winds. NWS Storm Survey results noted that the small buildings were light and not well anchored down, that the metal pole barn was open on the ends, and that the stick-built barn was old and also had a door open - allowing winds to get inside. All damage was laying uniformly towards the ENE.
Several locust trees were snapped along Wonderful Lane. However the NWS Storm Survey team noted that most of them had rotted trunks. All trees were uniformly laying to the east.

An older barn lost a large section of the roofing, causing one side to collapse. The roof sections were intact and traveled about 30 feet eastward, away from the barn. A large tree branch was also snapped in the same location.
Multiple large tree limbs between 5 and 7 inches in diameter were downed due to thunderstorm winds. Trees did not appear to be rotted, and were all laying uniformly towards the east.
A rotten oak tree was snapped.

A peg construction barn collapsed with most debris uniformly laying towards the ENE and NE. The roof was dislodged and tossed 150 feet to the east of the barn, but the framing of the roof seemed to be rotted. The cement footers that the bar was sitting on showed no indication of being anchored to the barn - rather the weight of the barn was holding it up.

A partial barn collapse. The walls of the barn did look to be anchored with a piece of rebarb sticking out of the concrete footers, and into a hole at the bottom of the 6x6 inch barn posts/vertical beams. No other anchoring clips were used, so wind was able to lift post off the anchor. The NWS Storm Survey Team also noted that most of the wood was dry rotted.

A barn was moved off its foundation and lost its roof. According to the NWS Storm Survey Steam, the cement block footers showed no indication of anchors to the barn and the wood looked dry rotted. Remainders of the barn were through 1/8 mile in a uniform direction to the ENE.
An open air barn had its roof peeled off and thrown into the field east of the barn. The NWS Storm Survey Team noted that the wood of the barn was dry rotted and weathered.

The National Park Service YELK2 RAWS site at Cumberland Gap recorded 1.68 inches of rainfall in 1 hour.
The MDLK2 U.S. Army Corps of Engineers observation site recorded a one hour rainfall total of 1.96 inches.

Middlesboro Police Department reported the closure of Highway 25E at Hardees due to flash flooding.

Bell County had one storm total snowfall observation during the event - 2 miles SSW of Beverly first reported having met warning criteria with 4.0 inches of snow measured at 7pm on 15th. By the next morning, the storm total snowfall was 4.8 inches at the same location.

Reports in excess of 4 inches (Winter Storm Warning Criteria) were made in several locations around Breathitt County by the early morning hours of January 15. Multiple locations reported between 4.1 and 4.7 inches. With a second wave of snow, snow totals increased to 7.1 inches in Jackson proper by that evening (report made at 7:10pm). The final storm total snowfall measurement at the Jackson, KY NWS office was 8.7 inches at 7am on January 16.
A measurement of 4.6 inches came in from Oneida in Clay County at 7am on January 16.
A report of 4.0 inches of storm total snowfall was made 9 miles SSE of Olive Hill at 9am on January 16, reaching the Winter Storm Warning snowfall criteria.

Official storm total snowfall reports for Estill County ranged from 3.2 inches at 8am on January 16 in the community of Cressy in the northern part of the county, to 4.8 inches at 10am in the community of Wagersville, in the southern half of the county. Meanwhile, on the 15th, the community of Doe Creek had already measured 5.0 inches as of 9:20am (report via Twitter). By 10:00pm (almost 12 hours later), the total was up to 5.9 inches.

Floyd County was in one of the heaviest areas of the snow. By 9am on January 15, several locations had already met or topped warning criteria of 4 inches. By 2pm, the community of Emma reported 4.3 inches of snow. A cooperative observer 2 miles ENE of Dotson reported 4 inches of snowfall at 1pm at their location, increasing to 5.3 inches by 8pm that evening. At 8:40pm, a viewer of WSAZTV reported 5 inches of snow in Prestonsburg thus far as well. Multiple storm total snowfall reports from various sources came in from across the county during the morning of January 16 as well. Accumulations generally ranged from 5.5 inches in Hippo (9:45am Jan. 16), to 7.3 inches 1 mile SE of Bosco (10am Jan. 16). Additional reports from Floyd County included 5.8 inches 2 miles S of Grethel, reported at 7:30am; 6 inches in Grethel at 9:45 am; 6.8 inches 1 WSW of Prestonsburg at 9am; 6.9 inches 2 WSW of Prestonsburg at 7am; 7.0 inches in Hi Hat at 9:45am; 7.0 inches at East Point at 9:45am; and 7 inches in Prestonsburg proper at 9am.

Multiple observations were made across Harlan County on January 16, ranging from 3.5 inches in Harlan proper at 10am, to 7.5 inches in the higher elevations 3 miles N of Harlan at 9:16am. Other reports from the county included 5.4 inches 5 miles NE of Baxter at 7am; 5 inches in the community of Blair at 9:31am; and 4.3 inches 1 mile S of Harlan at 6am.

Several reports from January 15 showed locations in Jackson County had already topped 4 inches (warning criteria). Sandgap reported around 4 inches of snow as of 9:15am on the 15th (they then reported another 0.8 inches of snow had fallen by that evening). A trained spotter reported 4.5 inches of snow as of 4:50pm 2 miles NNW of Loam. By the next morning, Storm Total Snowfall reports on January 16 ranged from 5.5 inches 1 mile S of Eglon at 8am, to 7 inches in McKee at 9:45am. Elsewhere in the county reports included 6 inches at Sandgap at 9am and 5.5 inches also 8 miles W of McKee at 7:59am.

Amounts were fairly uniform across Johnson County on the morning of January 16. A 6.0 inch report was received 1 mile E of Paintsville at 7am (this was an increase from a 4.0 report 24 hours earlier). Meanwhile, 6.5 inches was reported at 3 different sites - West Van Lear at 8:35am, Van Lear at 9:30am; and 2 miles WSW of Galen at 9:45am. A spotter report also came in the day before, on January 15 at 10:08pm, which stated that 5.5 inches of snow had fallen 1 mile NW of Auxier, near Prestonsburg, and it was still snowing at the time of the report.
One report was received from Kott County - from the community of Carrie. They measured 5 inches at 8am on January 16.
The cooperative observer in Barbourville reported a snowfall measurement of 4.5 inches at 9:30am on January 16.

A cooperative observer 4 miles N of Beattyville reported a total of 5.5 inches at 9:16am on January 16. This was an increase from 3.5 inches reported the morning before on the 15th around the same time. Meanwhile, there were also 2 additional reports given on January 15 with some pretty high amounts. At 12:45pm, public reported 6.0 inches of snow 1 mile ESE of Athol. Then at 7:35pm, there was a public report of 7.0 inches of snow measured in the community of Athol on Highland Road.
A report of 6.3 inches of snow was made from the community of Thousandsticks at 8:06 am on the 16th.

Two storm total reports came in from Magoffin County, both reading 6.5 inches. The first was made at 8am by the Salyersville Water Works (this is an increase from the 3.0 inches measured the morning before). The community of Hendricks was the second report at 10am (an increase from 4 inches reported the morning before).

A cooperative observer 2 miles E of Inez reported a storm total snowfall of 6.4 inches at 7:00am on January 16 (this is an increase from 2.5 inches measured the morning before around the same time). Inez proper also reported 7.0 inches at 10am on January 16.
A cooperative observer reported 4.9 inches of storm total snowfall at 8am on January 16 5 miles E of Crockett. This is an increase from 2.6 inches 24 hours before.

Owsley County had the highest total snowfall report out of this event. The observation point 4 ENE of Booneville recorded 9.3 inches of snow as of 7am on January 16. This was an increase from 4.5 inches reported 24 hours before. Also on the 15th, a CoCoRaHS station 2 miles NNW of Lerose reported a similar 4.3 inches of snow had already fallen as of 7:30am.

Multiple storm total reports were made in Perry County on January 16, ranging from 6.3 to 8.5 inches. These reports include 6.3 inches storm total 2 miles NW of Daisy at 10am, 6.8 inches at Hazard Water Works at 7am (up from only 1.3 inches measured the morning before), and 8.5 inches 1 mile SSW of Ary at 9:20am.||Meanwhile, the day before (January 15), there were several reports that already exceeded the warning threshold, including a public report of 4.3 inches from 2 miles SE of Ned at 11:50am, an amateur radio report of 4.5 inches of snow in Hazard around 4:30pm, and another of 7.0 inches 2 miles ENE of Lamont around 5:39pm.
Two storm total reports were made in Pike County on January 16 at 10am. The first was for 6.9 inches in the community of Whitepost, and the second was for 6.0 inches in Pikeville proper.

Several storm total snowfall reports made in Pulaski County on January 16 ranged from 4 inches to 7.3 inches. 4 miles SSE of Burnside was the big winner with 7.3 inches of snow as of 7am (they had reported 3.6 inches the morning before). Eubank reported 5.5 inches at 9:35am, and 1 SW of the Pulaski County Park reported 4.0 inches at 9:45am.
One storm total report of 4.5 inches was received from 1 NE of Williamsburg at 10am on January 16.

While no storm total reports were made on January 16, two reports came on on the 15th which were exceeding warning criteria. At 4:30pm, an amateure radio operator reported 4.2 inches of snow so far in the community of Keavy. A little later at 6:45pm, broadcast media reported 5 inches of snow 2 miles south of the London-Corbin Airport.

While no storm total snowfall reports were made on January 16, there were a couple reports from the day before that exceeded warning criteria. 4.0 inches of snow was reported by the pubic at 9:45am 1 mile NNE of Hollonville (Terrell Fork Road Community). Later that day, broadcast media reported 6.1 inches of snow at 8:45pm in the community of Bethany.
A member of the public reported 4 inches of snowfall near the Monticello area at 2:20pm on January 15. This is not the storm total snowfall through 16th, but still met warning criteria.

While there were no storm total snowfall reports for Letcher County on January 16th, there was a report that verified the Winter Storm Warning the evening before. An amateur radio operator reported 4.5 inches of snow had fallen so far as of 7:53pm January 15 in the community of Blackey.

The reports of snowfall started coming in for Rowan County on the morning of the 19th. At 7am, a cooperative observer located 2 miles SSE of Farmers reported 4 inches. By 7:30am, a member of the public in Morehead reported 4.5 inches on social media. Then by 10am, the total was up to 6 inches in Morehead. At 12:30pm, 5 inches was reported by the emergency manager 2 miles NNE of the Lakeview Heights area. Shortly after, the community of Hilda also reported 6.0 inches.

At 10am on the 19th, an NWS employee reported 3.5 inches of snow 1 mile S of Oggs Station, just shy of warning criteria. However as snow continued to fall, by noon the public made a report in a similar location (1 mile SW of Oggs Station) of 4.0 inches measured - officially reaching winter warning criteria.

A member of the public reported 4 inches of measured snowfall as of 7pm on the 19th. Most other locations across the county saw between 1 and 2 inches as of 7am that morning, with snow continuing through the day.

Multiple reports of between 2 and 3 inches of snow came in during the morning hours in Estill County. However, as the snow continued to fall in some locations, a member of the public located 1 mile NNW of Evelyn sent in a picture via social media of 6 inches haven fallen as of 12:55pm. Meanwhile, another location in the county (Weedon) only had 3.3 inches as of 9:45pm that evening - showing the variability across the county.
A CoCoRaHS observer located near Olive Hill (3 miles ENE of Stark) measured 5 inches of snow as of 9am on January 19. This was the only report that was made for Elliott County.
An amateur radio operator sent in a report of 4.8 inches of snowfall in Sharpsburg as of 10:27am.

A tree was reported down along the 1000 block of Dry Creek Road near Clearfield.
A tree was blown down at the intersection of Robin Hood Drive and Knapp Avenue.
A barn was blown down at Route 11 and Van Thompson Road in the community of Judy.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 67 mph was measured at the ASOS at the London-Corbin Airport with storms that went through in the morning.
The Kentucky Mesonet station on top of Black Mountain in Harlan County measured a wind gust of 57 mph.
A tree was blown down on Maddox Street, just northeast of Flemingsburg.
A tree was reported down on Doe Creek Road. The exact location along the road was not given.
A tree was reported down at 265 Cobhill Road near the community of Pryse.
A barn was blown down along White Oak road, approximately 1 mile from Wyoming Road, north of Owingsville.
A tree was blown down onto a power line at 155 McKenzie Road just SW of Farmers.
Montgomery County Dispatch reported a tree blown down by thunderstorm winds. The tree was blocking Nest Egg Road near the intersection of Summer Ridge Road.
Bath County dispatch reported a tree blown down onto telephone lines near the intersection of US-60 and Moores Ferry Road.

The NWS Survey team determined that damage incurred near the community of Deering was consistent with straight line winds, with maximum wind gusts estimated to be between 80 and 90 mph. The most significant damage occurred to a barn just off Akins Lane, about 7 miles SW of Corbin - in which the barn was destroyed. There were numerous trees uprooted between Frankfort School Road and Bee Creek Road, and from there to Linda Lane, just off Casey Road. Several homes sustained damage from trees that fell on roofs. Of notable interest were eyewitness reports of a circulation that tracked across a small pond in one of the residential areas. Based on the description of the circulation not being in contact with the cloud base, and the location of this event over a pond approximately 300 years off the flanking (west) side of the core of the most destructive winds, the NWS believes this may have been a book-end vortex.
A tree was blown down onto a pickup and farm outbuildings via a public report with photo relayed by broadcast media.
Harlan County dispatch relayed a report of a downed tree on US-119 near MM28.
Rowan County dispatch reported a tree was down at the intersection of Christy Creek Road and Pattys Lick Road just east of Morehead.
Martin County dispatch relayed a report of a tree through a roof near the 2000 block of Tomahawk Road northwest of Inez.
Johnson County dispatch reported a tree down on US-40 about 2 miles from the Martin County line.
Johnson County dispatch reported a tree blocking KY-172 near the 1930 block in Staffordsville.
A public report of half dollar sized hail was received near the Bell County High School.
Multiple trees were downed at the north end of Cave Run Lake near the dam.
A tree was reported blown down onto US-421 in the vicinity of Chat Branch Road near the community of Garrard.
A tree was blown down onto US-421 near the intersection with Clay-Leslie Industrial Park Road.
A tree was blown down and blocking Skyline View Road southeast of London.
Downed trees and powerlines along the 800 block of KY-700 (Sandhill Road), NNE of Whitley City.
Powerlines were down along the 800 block of US-27 north in Whitley City.
A tree was downed on US-460 in Ezel according to a social media report.
A roof was blown off a storage building near the community of Hilda.
Multiple trees are down on KY-11 near the community of Bowen, along with large limbs up to 4 inches in diameter.
A large chunk of roof was taken out of a barn in an exposed field east of the community of Stoops. Across the street was a second barn on Van Thompson Road with the door panels hanging loose.

A quick spin up occurred as winds descended to the ground in NW Bath County, hitting a house on top of a ridge off of Springfield Road (south of Sharpsburg), along with trees and a barn in the adjacent holler to the east. From this point forward, the event became more straight-line wind dominated and continued to be so throughout much of the county. The house sustained substantial damage. A large section of roofing was removed, including a large hole into the master closet. All windows around entire house had been bowed in, bending the frames and cracking the molding around them. Grass, dirt, insulation, and other small debris was also plastered to windows, doors, and siding on all sides of the house, including on all sides of a sheltered screen in porch. Flashing was also removed from inside the sheltered porch. Basement doors on other side of sheltering retaining wall were buckled in by the force of the wind (and possible change in pressure). House also had multiple cracks along the exterior brick-work that were not there before. In addition, it moved several things outside, including a large trailer holding the front of a combine, twisting the tongue of the trailer. Debris from the house was blown several hundred yards away, and some has not yet been found. Farther down from the house, numerous trees and a barn was hit. The barn is still standing, but sustained substantial damage to the SE corner.
Swath of wind went through fields, passing through Gossett Road in a path about 600 yards long. Numerous trees were snapped along the tree lines and along the road, with all debris laying eastward.
Roofing was peeled off of west side of the barn, along with multiple large tree limbs snapped on the property along Flat Creek Road. Another barn behind this one also sustained roof damage.

Farm sustained heavy wind damage along W Hwy-60. An open air barn collapsed. Metal roof from the barn was thrown southward and eastward about 200-300 yards across fields. Multiple Bradford Pear trees were also broken, and several other sheds were damaged.

A historic brick house built in 1820 sustained substantial straight-line wind damage. The house is situated on an elevated knob with a large open area to the west, unable to break the wind before hitting the house. Owner describes seeing strong straight-line winds heading towards his house from west to east. When the winds hit the house, they knocked out one of the chimneys and roof apex on the west facing side of the house, causing a large amount of damage both outside and inside of the historic home. Several very large pine trees also fell, including one that hit a window on the house where the owner was standing. In addition to the house, winds destroyed a barn located to the south of the house, along with several sheds. The survey team and owner noted that all trees and debris was pushed due east by the winds. The team also noted that this was by far the worst damage sustained from this event, likely due to the property's elevated and exposed location.
Roofing was peeled off and wall caved in on a barn along Preston Road (CR-965), south of Owingsville. In addition, the Dollar General across the road to the NW also sustained some minor damage.

Strong winds hit a barn in an open field from the west on KY-36 just NW of Olympia, blowing off the barn roof and throwing it eastward. The barn was also pushed off it's foundation, partially exposing the classic cars it was housing. Metal roofing was blown several hundred yards to the east.

Strong easterly winds led to substantial damage for a garage and mobile home along Lafafette Road in the community of Olympia. Both structures were facing westward, taking the brunt of the impact. The mobile home sustained porch and roof damage. The large metal-framed garage had bay doors on both the west/frontward and east/rear facing sides. Winds caused the west facing doors to bow in, and the east facing doors to blow out.

An old barn and several sheds sustained major damage at the end of Lafafette Road in the community of Olympia. The main barn lost the majority of it's roofing and had the collapse of walls, though still standing. Several nearby sheds were also destroyed, with debris blown out to the east. Multiple trees were also broken in the area. Meanwhile, a neighboring new barn frame being built about 100 yards to the north received little to no damage.
A small concrete blocked building housing an auction company lost its tin roof, thrown eastward. The building was located near the intersection of KY-36 and KY-11 between Sharpsburg and Bethel.

A barn sustained wind damage along Market Lane, near KY-11, between Sharpsburg and Bethel. The barn was already structurally unsound, but the additional winds collapsed the barn, throwing pieces of the roofing and wood sides across KY-11 about 100+ yards to the east.
Plastic greenhouse covers were pulled off at an Amish house along Shields Road near Reynoldsville.

House sustained damage along Mt. Pleasant Road just north of Reynoldsville. The house was located on the northside of a spin-up tornado. Two sheds behind the house collapsed and were thrown ENE, with contents and metal roofing littering the yard and across the street to the east. The southeast corner of the house also was missing roofing material off the porch, and the south-side of the porch was ripped off. Owners also reported that some of the windows bowed in, likely due to the nearby tornado.

Straight line winds pushed through Mount Pleasant Road from west to east, resulting in damage to structures on both the north and south side of this mobile home. However, the mobile home, which set in the middle of the damage, showed signs of rotation as the system moved through, indicative of a quick spin-up tornado. All damage that was viewed downstream by the survey team seemed to be more in line with straight-line winds as well, so this was likely a very quick spin-up. There was a lack of structures behind this mobile home, and a lack of damage across the street to the east of this home. It matched up well with one of the tighter circulations that went through the area. The mobile home itself was hit from the backside, lifting off the roof on the back half of the house. Siding was torn off on all sides. The front of the house's roofline was a bit rotted, but lost it's flashing. Insulation and mud was plastered along the front side. Meanwhile, more mud and insulation was plastered all through the inside of the house as well.

Multiple trees were snapped and twisted along the tree line down Tower Road in the community of White Oak. Most of the trees were laying to the N or NW. Utility crews were also working at the end of Tower Road, though there were no signs of visible damage here.
An older barn collapsed due to strong winds. It's was located in an exposed and elevated landscape.

A very large but rotted tree fell eastward due to the straight line winds, landing on the corner of a manufactured home and destroying it along Hillsboro Road, near the intersection with Naylor Road. Behind the house, sat an older barn, which was pushed from behind by the easterly winds, moving it forward about 10 feet off the foundation and causing it to collapse.

A west-facing porch was pulled off the back of a well-tied down doublewide manufactured home when strong east winds hit it along Hillsboro Road in the Slate Valley community. This resulted in further roof damage. Two large softwood trees were also snapped. Two houses down, a shed was also destroyed, and another house across the street received minor roof damage.
Large pine tree snapped around the limb base along Riddle Road near the intersection with Forge Hill Road in the Peasticks community.
Multiple healthy hardwood trees were snapped along Old Sands Road (KY-1269) in the Peasticks Community. Trees were all laying ENE or E.

A property along Old Sand Road near I-64, east of the Peasticks community, received multiple points of damage. The home owner recalled seeing a wall of wind come from the east straight at them. The corner of the barn was destroyed, and roofing material also removed. Soffits, gutters, and some siding was pulled off the back of the house. A shed was lifted up and destroyed. A neighbor's shed had the same fate. Multiple trees were also blown down, hitting the fence at the front of the house.

NWS Survey team found a section along Old Sand Road where over 15 trees were uprooted and snapped, including healthy hardwoods and softwoods. All the trees were laying to the east. Meanwhile, a fairly old trailer was in the middle of the damage and seemed to be fine.
A couple of pine trees were snapped and blown eastward across Vance Road, north of Polksville.
Easterly winds hit the back of a metal lean-to on Polksville Road (north of Polksville), throwing tin roofing across the yard and road to the east.
A tree located at a house on the west side of Moores Ferry Road, just before the intersection with Vance Road and I-64, received considerable wind damage, knocking out about a third of the tree.

A business along Moores Ferry Road, just northeast of Polksville, sustained multiple points of damage. Numerous hardwoods were snapped and laying eastward, along with even more branches. In addition, a small open-air shed was uplifted off the gravel lot and blown up and over the fence to the southeast.

The survey team was sent to a property that sustained substantial damage off Chandler road just NE of the Bethel community. Two houses set on the property next to one another. The first was an old farmhouse that was being lived in but no longer maintained. The house directly beside it was a new Amish house. When winds hit the older house, sitting to the west, it lifted off the roof structure and threw it to the ESE, hitting the roof and chimney of the new house. This caused the chimney to collapse and fall, leading to significant damage to the side of the house and porches. Thankfully no one was injured in this incident. In addition, several other nearby outbuildings sustained damage, as did the siding on the houses, but all other structures on the property were fine.

Two barns set beside each other at the start of Chandler Road, near Shiloh Road, one an open air newer barn on the NW side, and the other a large old wooden white barn just to the SE. Wind hit the open air barn and caused it to collapse, though no notable damage appears to be sustained to the white barn next to it.

A small subdivision along Country Lane in Bethel sustained damage due to straight line winds. Several houses had Bradford Pear Trees and rotted hardwood trees that blew down to the east. Several homes also sustained shingle and minor roof damage on the west facing side. In addition, a small timber frame that was being built (likely a shed) collapsed.

The east side of a barn roof was blown off along Johnson School Road in southern Fleming County. Additional damage to roof panels was incurred on the west side of the barn. Pieces of roofing were thrown eastward and along the road. In addition, the house directly across the street received minor damage as well, including the gutters being torn off the east side of the house. Several large tree limbs also looked to have been downed.  This location was in a flat exposed location, and no other structures nearby.
Many trees were snapped and limbs broken along ridge parallel to KY-158, and up onto Markwell Road.
Several trees were downed at Ringo Mills Baptist Church on KY-158 near Hillsboro. In addition, the church sustained minor exterior damage to the roof and gutters.
Numerous trees were broken or snapped along KY-211 just SE of Linville Road. In addition, an older mobile home (possibly vacant) on the east side of the road sustained visible damage.

A large and empty farm silo along KY-1722, near the intersection with KY-211, sustained wind damage to the west side. The wind hit the silo and indented it, making it look like it took a punch. No other debris or damage was noted in the area.

The side and top of a barn was blown off along KY-1722 near the Licking River. Most of the debris was blown eastward across the road and into the trees across the street. In addition, numerous trees behind the barn and along the river received broken limbs as the wind came through.

The survey team found numerous trees uprooted and snapped between Bluebank Road and I-64, near the intersection of L. Stevens Road. The trees were generally felled to the NE, some crossing Bluebank Road and blocking the road.

A large pine tree was uprooted in front of a house on Bluebank Road, just north of the intersection with Ramey Ridge Road. The tree fell southward, hitting the front porch of the house. The extent of the damage is unknown.

A metal barn behind a house on Shawnee Drive had a door and panels blown out on the north side. The team was unable to see the remainder of the back of the barn from their location. It also appeared as though the house, located east of the barn, had some windows blown out on the garage doors, however it is unclear if the damage occurred from the storm.

A house on the east side of Shawnee Drive sustained minor damage, with the flashing being removed from the front westward facing side, as well as the south side of a house. The team was unable to see the backside of the house for any additional damage.

A house on the west side of Shawnee Drive, near the intersection with KY-158, sustained considerable damage when strong easterly winds struck the chimney on the southwest side. The chimney collapsed into the roof structure, losing it's stone fa��ade. In addition, a metal garage (located on the north side of the house) sustained damage to the east facing large garage door. The garage door had been removed at time of survey. Meanwhile, the house next door (north of above-mentioned house/west side of the street) received siding damage to the south-facing side of the house, and had it's AC unit flipped over on the same side. The house across the street also sustained a broken window, and missing shingles/flashing.

Several points of damage located along KY-158 just past Shawnee Drive. A wooden barn had it's barn door broken, along with peeling roof panels. A large hardwood tree was also uprooted on the property. Across the street, to the south, a house lost it's downspout. The County EM also informed that another house in this vicinity lost a front porch column in the storm, but it had since been put back in place.
Multiple trees were downed along KY-58, between Derrickson Road and Parker Lane, facing eastward.
A metal barn/garage located on KY-158 near Flemingsburg Road sustained wind damage. Metal sheets from the barn were throw eastward, including roofing, flashing, and side panels.
The survey team surveyed a RV park along Rosetown Church Road near the community of Youngs Creek. The park had multiple trees uprooted, and RVs that were toppled and/or destroyed.
Several hardwood trees uprooted and snapped, some rotted, along Frankfort School Road, between Rosetown Church Road and Tom Taylor Road. Damage direction was generally N.

Multiple trees were uprooted on a property along Frankfort School Road. One of the trees fell onto the house on the property, causing considerable damage. However, the house was vacant at the time and already in a deteriorating shape.
A swath of trees along the tree line between Ottis Ward Road and Frankfort School Road were damaged, some snapped and some losing large branches.

The National Weather Service surveyed damage in the Siler |community, on the eastern edge of Corbin. They confirmed, with the|help of video, that a quick spin-up tornado occurred, starting in|the NW corner of the Legacy Chevrolet dealership's parking lot, |affecting a gas station and car wash, then moving ENE across |US-25E, into a manufactured shed retail lot. It then crossed into |a tree line and adjacent field, possibly lifting momentarily, |before resuming damage near Poplar Grove Road. It then traveled |between Lynn Camp High School and Lynn Camp Elementary School, |before dissipating. Notable damage included damage to to vehicles |in the Legacy Chevrolet parking lot. Multiple cars and trucks |were pushed forward or to the side. The line of trucks near the |front of the lot were pushed up over the curb and halfway into the |grass. Debris was located along the seal of the driver-side |window of multiple trucks, and quite a few vehicles lost their|back windshields either partially or completely. The gas cap |covers were pulled off of the trucks, with some found at the end of the|tornado path about 0.75 miles away. The neighboring car wash lost|the majority of its windows and incurred damage to all sides of |the building, causing it to be structurally unsound. Across the |street, sheds and barns were moved around and flipped, including a|metal carport being thrown into the tree line to the ENE. No damage|was noted along the neighboring field, however minor roof damage |and a fallen tree occurred just to the ENE, at which point the |path of damage picked back up with multiple trees down along |Poplar Grove Road. At the end of the tornado track, a south-facing|house addition had its roof and ceiling lifted off, landing in |it's entirety to the north near the Lynn Camp Elementary School, |while additional debris was thrown into the east facing lawn of |the school. ||The track of this storm started at Cumberland Falls State Park, |moving east-northeast, resulting in a path of straight-line wind |damage across northern Whitley County with numerous trees felled.|NWS Jackson, KY radar showed a tightening of circulation occurring|across the Corbin area, near where the tornado occurred. Further |wind damage was noted farther ENE of the tornado path in a wooded |area along Middlefork Richland Road and surrounding areas. These |were all indicative of straight-line winds as well.

Two observing stations in Bath County, a Kentucky Mesonet station 3 miles south of Owingsville and the other a personal weather station 2 miles northwest of Owingsville, recorded peak wind gusts of 45 and 47 mph, respectively. Even so, multiple reports from the Bath County dispatch of trees and power lines blown down around the county suggest instances of stronger wind gusts. One of those reports at 1120 AM EST indicated that a tree fell onto a structure.

One observing station at the Middlesboro Airport reported a peak gust of 43 mph at 935 AM EST. Even so, there were, according to Bell County dispatch, many reports of trees blown down in the county, primarily after 200 PM EST in the Pineville, Frakes, Middlesboro and Brownies Creek areas. A trained spotter also reported a tree blown down off of KY-2011 near the intersection with Cow Fork Road around 1245 PM EST.

Five observing stations in Breathitt County reported wind gusts, though peak speeds differed dramatically due to exposure. The strongest recorded wind gust of 56 mph occurred around 318 PM EST at the NWS Jackson ASOS. Meanwhile, the adjacent Jackson RAWs recorded a peak gusts of 41 mph at 956 AM EST. Other reported peak wind gusts ranged from 20 mph in a sheltered hollow 2 miles ENE of Noble at 1035 AM EST to 41 mph 2 miles SSE Noble at 215 PM EST. Wind damage was reported around the county by law enforcement, NWS employees and the public. These reports include: 1045 AM EST - trees blown down in the Frozen community; 1050 AM EST - trees blown down near WFO Jackson and on KY-30 within a couple miles of the offices, shingles were also blown off the NWS office building; 1100 AM EST - trees blown down on KY-541 near the Martha Layne Collins Bridge; 200 PM EST - power line blown down KY-15 immediately southeast of the Wolfe/Breathitt county line; 315 PM EST - tree blown down in Jackson, and 318 PM EST - tree blown down on KY-30 West about 1 mile from old KY-15, tree blown down onto vehicle along KY-315 approximately 3 miles from KY-30. Pictures on social media also show a large hardwood tree down at the Kentucky Mountain Bible College, impacting one of the college buildings.

The only observing station in the county, the Peabody RAWS reported a peak wind gusts of 28 mph at 601 PM EST.  However the station is likely sited very poorly. The county dispatch reported that trees and utility lines had been blown down in Manchester with numerous trees knocked over in other parts of the county. There were reportedly additional occurrences of downed utility lines as well.
Estill County dispatch reported multiple trees and power lines blown down across the county at 930 AM EST.

One personal weather observing station 2 miles northeast Poplar Plains reported a peak gust of 48 mph at 1114 AM EST. The Fleming-Mason Airport just north of the county reported a peak gusts of 54 mph at 1135 AM EST. Localized damage suggests instances of higher wind gusts. The local COOP observer WRIM2 reported roofing blown off of a nearby residence as well as a blown over carport.

Floyd County dispatch and members of the public reported that trees were blown down in the Prestonsburg, Blue River, David, McDowell, Martin, Grethel, Betsy Layne and Harold areas, primarily during the morning hours.

Two observing stations in Harlan County, one Kentucky Mesonet station atop Big Black Mountains and one AWOS station at the Harlan County Airport, reported peak wind gusts of 45 and 38 mph, respectively. Even so, localized wind damage suggests that there were isolated instances of high gusts. Law enforcement reported multiple instances of trees and power lines blown down in the Cawood, Evarts, and Cumberland areas during the morning hours. In Cawood, one of those trees, a large pine tree, fell onto a mobile home in Cawood, injuring one occupant.

One Kentucky Mesonet station 5 miles south of McKee reported a peak wind gusts of 47 mph at 930 AM EST. Even so, Jackson County dispatch received multiple reports of trees blown down in portions of the county, suggesting higher wind gusts.

The Kentucky Mesonet station 4 miles west of Paintsville reported a peak wind gust of 39 mph at 1130 AM EST. Locally higher wind gusts likely occurred given substantial siding damage inflicted on the 6th floor of the high-rise Bristlebuck Manor in the city of Paintsville.

The Kentucky Mesonet station located 5 miles north of Hindman reported a peak gust of 44 mph at 940 AM EST. Law enforcement reported instances of multiple trees blown down in the Vest and Pippa Passes communities suggesting that locally higher gusts probably occurred.

The Kentucky Mesonet station 3 miles east of Barbourville reported a peak wind gust of 35 mph at 240 PM EST. The Knox County dispatch received multiple reports of trees and powerlines blown down around the county, suggesting that isolated higher gusts likely occurred.

The ASOS weather station at the London-Corbin Airport reported a peak wind gust of 49 mph during the morning hours. However most of the reports of downed trees, up to around 20 according to Laurel County dispatch, occurred between 1100 AM EST and 300 PM EST and were most numerous in the City of London as well as Swiss Colony and Bald Rock.
The Lee County dispatch reported that multiple trees and powerlines had been blown down throughout the county.

The Leslie County dispatch reported that trees had been blown down in the Essie area along KY-406, in the vicinity of Hyden, and on KY-2058 near Beech Fork. A single tree was reportedly blown down on Big Valley Road north of the Hal Rogers Parkway. Utility lines were brought down in the Essie area.

Two weather observing stations, a personal weather station 1 mile northeast of Payne Gap and a Kentucky Mesonet station 2 miles northwest of Whitesburg, reported wind gusts of 41 mph at 1112 AM EST and 29 mph at 845 AM EST, respectively. Even so, Letcher County dispatch reported that there were multiple trees blown down in the Jenkins, Whitesburg, and Fleming-Neon areas.

The AWOS station at the Big Sandy Airport reported a peak wind gust of only 36 mph at 1135 AM EST. However, Martin County dispatch reported that there were instances of trees and powerlines blown down across all of the county.

The Kentucky Mesonet station 3 miles north of Whitley City reported a peak wind gust of 30 mph at 225 PM EST. However, the Whitley County dispatch reported that multiple trees and a utility line were blown down at both near Whitley City and Pine Knot, suggesting that locally higher wind gusts occurred.

The Kentucky Mesonet station 6 miles south southwest of Frenchburg reported a peak wind gust of 42 mph at 1010 AM EST. However, damage observed by an NWS Employee suggests that higher wind gusts occurred. A large tree had snapped at ground level and fallen towards a home at the intersection of US-460 and Industrial Park Road, damaging the home's porch. Two trees were also blown down along Tuffy Stull Road. Another tree fell and blocked US-460 near the intersection of Dog Trot Road. Power outages due to fallen trees persisted for multiple days after the storm system's passage.

Two weather stations, a personal weather station 1 miles northwest of Ewington and the AWOS at the Mount Sterling Airport, reported peak wind gusts of 52 mph at 1204 PM EST and 48 mph at 1215PM EST, respectively. In spite of these gusts not attaining warning criteria, widespread wind damage was reported by NWS employees around the county. At 1030 AM EST, an NWS employee reported a tree blown down onto and blocking High Street one block east of the courthouse. At least 2 trees were blown down along US-460 near Camargo and multiple trees were blown down onto KY-646 at the intersection with KY-213, blocking the highway and involving the power lines. Another  large hardwood, approximately 18-inch diameter, was snapped off at its base at the intersection of KY-213 and Shelby Lane. Additionally, a large yard tree fell through the main section of a home in Mount Sterling near the Maysville Community and Technical College. Approximately half a dozen consecutive power poles were snapped along US-460 immediately southeast of the intersection with KY-686. Finally, a large yard tree was uprooted and fallen on a livestock fence on the southwest side of US-460 adjacent to Hartzler Door and Gate.

The Kentucky Mesonet station 2 miles southwest of West Liberty recorded a peak wind gusts of 60 mph at 1130 AM EST. An NWS employee also reported a tree blown down on KY-946 about a mile and half from Maytown.

The AWOS at Wendell H. Ford Airport recorded a peak wind gust of 38 mph at 235 PM EST. However, wind damage reported by the the highway department in Perry County suggests that higher wind gusts occurred. Reports included a large tree blown down onto KY-699 and blocking the highway near the old Leatherwood school. Multiple trees were reportedly blown down along KY-15 North in the vicinity of the Wendell H. Ford Airport and also on Left Fork of Maces Creek about 2.5 miles from KY-7. Single downed trees were reported onto KY-476 near the intersection with Balls Fork Road and along KY-15 at the Breathitt-Perry county line.

Two weather stations, the Pike County Airport and the Kentucky Mesonet station 3 miles south of Pikeville, recorded peak wind gusts of 52 mph at 955 AM EST and 57 mph at 200 PM EST, respectively. Wind damage around the county suggests that locally higher wind gusts occurred. The Pike County emergency manager reported that a tree fell on a residence on the Right Fork of Sycamore Road near Ashcamp around 927 AM EST. Another tree was blown down onto a residence along Taylor Road in Zebulon around 955 AM EST. Reports were also received of individual trees blown down near the intersections of KY-610 and Elwood Road, Town Mountain Road and Lothlorien Lane, and also onto KY-1526 in the Zebulon community between Double Kwik and Velocity Market. An NWS employee reported that there were multiple trees blown down in Ridge Line Road between River Hurricane Branch and KY-194.

National Weather Service employees reported multiple trees blown down in the county. One of those reports was of a tree uprooted at a residence 1 mile east northeast of Clay City at 1005 AM EST. A tree was also blown down and blocking KY-615 in the vicinity of Courtney Lane. Broadcast media reported that a roof was blown off of a mobile home.

Three weather stations, the RAWS on Triangle Mountain, the AWOS at the Morehead Regional Airport and the Kentucky Mesonet 4 miles northeast of Morehead, reported peak wind gusts of 35 to 41 mph between 915 AM EST and 102 PM EST. Even though these reports are not particularly notable, a trained spotter near Farmers reported that 5 large poplar trees were uprooted. An mPING report also indicated that trees had been uprooted and a roof blown off about 1 miles southeast of Morehead.

Three weather stations, a Kentucky Mesonet station 4 miles northwest of Monticello, an AWOS at the Monticello Airport, and a personal weather station a the Conley Bottom Resort reported peak wind gusts of 35 to 41 mph between 235 PM EST and 345 PM EST. Isolated higher gusts likely occurred. Wayne County dispatch reported that a tree was blown down onto KY-92 near intersection with Dug Road and the intersection with Burnett Hollow Road. Multiple trees were reportedly blown down onto KY-3284 about 2 miles from the Monticello city limits.

The AWOS station at the Williamsburg-Whitley County Airport reported a peak wind gusts of 33 mph at 235 PM EST.  Locally higher gusts likely occurred along KY-92 along the northwest slope of Pine Mountain were multiple trees were blown down according to the Whitley County dispatch. Dispatch also reported that multiple trees were blown down on Corn Creek Church Road near the Knox-Whitley county line and that utility lines had been blown down in Williamsburg.
